video_title: How did a few hundred Spanish soldiers topple two empires? – Si Sheppard
transcript: Today I’m chatting with professor  and military historian Si Sheppard.  I want to talk to you about the  conquest of the Aztec and the Inca   Empires because these are some of the  most shocking events in human history,   unparalleled among all the military  and diplomatic achievements ever made.  A few hundred conquistadors show up to  a new continent they know nothing about.  Within a matter of years, they subjugate empires  which have millions of inhabitants in them.  In the process of doing so, they are often winning  battles where they are outnumbered 100 to 1,   1,000 to 1, and in many cases not  even taking a single casualty.  They’re doing this while upwards of 99% of their  fighting forces are made up of the very natives   that they’re going to subjugate. I wanted to have you on to talk   about something this episode. We’re not going to focus on it,   we’re mostly talking about history here,  but people think of AI takeover as this   crazy sci-fi scenario but this would not be the  first time in history that an alien force, with   motivations that the natives don’t understand, is  able to use diplomatic cunning and technological   advantages to outmaneuver and then take over  a much larger and well-established order.  I wanted to have you on to  understand what happened here.  First, I would love to hear the stories. What did Cortés do? What did Pizarro do?   How did these conquests actually go down? Thank you. It’s a great pleasure to be here.  Yes, we’re talking about the birth of our modern  world, which played out between 600 to 500   years ago and created the modern globalized  community that we all participate in today.  It began in the 15th century when Europe,  backed up against the wall of the Atlantic,   under immense pressure from external forces and  cut off from the core economic power bases of the   East — the sources of the spice and silk that had  driven the global economy historically throughout   Eurasia — was finally forced to innovate. Key names like Prince Henry the Navigator   of Portugal work on turning the Atlantic  Ocean from a barrier into a superhighway.  Generational knowledge accrued from captains  reporting on tides and wind currents and whatever   land they’ve managed to reconnoiter, building out  the map as they go along, enables them to find a   way around the southern tip of Africa directly  to India and therefore cut out the middleman.  The Spanish, meanwhile, are heading west. We all know the story of Christopher Columbus:   "In 1492, he sailed the ocean blue." That was entrepreneurship. This   was an expedition to arrive at the  Oriental markets by traveling west.  Of course, his figures were completely wrong. He was saved by the fact that, unknown to him,   there was an entire continent in the  place where he thought Japan, China,   and the Spice Islands would be. Initially, that was perceived,   ironically, as a disappointment. But over time, it became increasingly   apparent this was a source of potential in land,  in wealth, and in people that could be exploited.  A key turning point happened in 1511 when  an ambitious Spanish nobleman, de Velázquez,   seizes control of Cuba. He sends out from this power   base expeditions exploring the coast of what  we would call Mesoamerica, Central America.  Later in 1518, he assigns that task to a man  with whom he’s had a somewhat tempestuous   relationship, a man named Hernán Cortés. He’d arrived in the New World in Cuba in 1511.  He had some legal training, so he served as a  notary and worked his way up to being alcalde,   which is chief magistrate, on Cuba. But he had much greater ambition.  He takes this warrant from  the governor and runs with it.  He begins recruiting men to a much wider and  much more ambitious goal: not just to explore   the coast, but to penetrate into the interior, to  find out what’s there, and to seize control of it.  When the governor realizes what  Cortés is up to, he tries to stop him.  There’s this great moment on 18th November 1518. He arrives at the waterfront just as Cortés gets   into a boat to go out to his ships offshore. The governor calls out to him,   "What are you up to?" Cortés assures him, "Don’t worry.  I have this all under control." But of course, the governor   had lost control at that point. Now it was Cortés’s expedition.  This is the background. Again, as you say, he  is literally going off the side of the map.  He’s entering terra incognita,  unknown to Europeans previously.  His political antenna, honed by years in the  islands, enables him to appreciate at a very early   stage that there is a significant imperial power  which has hegemony here in the mainland, and that   its subject peoples chafe under the authority  of whoever this lord or imperial power is.  He arrives in the lands of the Totonacs, who had  recently been incorporated into the imperial orbit   of a people who call themselves the Mexica  — hence Mexico as we know it — but who have   come down to history based on their mythical  origins in a land called Aztlán as the Aztecs.  For simplicity’s sake, that’s  what we’ll refer to them as.  The Totonacs resented this authority, as  all subjugated and subordinated peoples do,   and they saw the arrival of these outsiders  as a potential opportunity to throw off the   authority that had been imposed on them. Having established this relationship with   the Totonacs, Cortés begins to march inland, and  he enters the territory of the Tlaxcalans, who,   like an autoimmune system, immediately rallied  to defeat him, to expel him from their territory.  But he fights them to a standstill for such  a period of time that the Tlaxcalans and he   arrive at a new kind of arrangement. The Tlaxcalans again appreciate his   strength, his power, his potential. They swing over to his side and will   henceforward serve as guides and reinforcements  for his expedition deeper into the interior.  Can we pause here and talk about the numbers? How many men had Cortés brought with him?  Even the Tlaxcalans had much  larger numbers than Cortés did.  So even the standstill is an impressive  military achievement, especially because   he’s fighting without native support. What are the numbers even at this point?  A few hundred on Cortés’ side and multiple  thousands on the Tlaxcalans’ side.  It’s at this point that the critical  technological differentials from the Old   and New World really begin to come into effect. The classic text which got me invested in this   whole scenario in the first place is Jared  Diamond’s book, Guns, Germs, and Steel.  He enumerates in the title those critical  advantages that the Spaniards had.  Guns in reality weren’t so significant. Once the Native peoples got over the shock value,   they appreciated, given the very slow reloading  times involved in firearms at that time,   that they weren’t so significant  as assets on the battlefield.  But steel was critical. Local weapons were carved  from wood and from stone and from obsidian, that   volcanic glass which is razor sharp when honed to  a point and quite dangerous as a slashing weapon.  But against the steel armor, and especially the  steel helmets that the conquistadors were wearing,   it was much less effective. The conquistadors were drawing   on military traditions of the Old World  that went back generations, incorporating   long Toledo steel sword blades. They used those as thrusting weapons to take   out indigenous warriors who were coming in with  cut-and-slash weapons, which of course open up   the side of the body to be taken out very early. The combination of the technology with generations   of inherited military training and  skill meant that the conquistadors   had that critical edge on the battlefield. Now, they weren’t invincible. Cortés was again   playing those mind games. He was taking casualties,   and he was careful to bury his dead underneath  the houses that they were sheltering in so the   Tlaxcalans wouldn’t be aware that they were even  having some successes in hand-to-hand combat.  It was as much a mind game  as it was a physical game.  The ultimate weapon, of course, that the  conquistadors brought with them was their horses.  I cannot overemphasize how vital the horse was  to the conquistadors once they entered into the   interior of the American continents. They had the external asset.  They had sail power, which enabled them  to land anywhere they wanted on the coast.  But in the interior, the horse was decisive. There were no native equivalents.  The horse originated in North America,  but it had subsequently died out.  The local peoples had not just no  horses, but no beast of burden generally.  That was not integrated into their economies,  into their ways of life, or into their military.  The Inca, whom we’ll discuss in a moment,  did have one, which was the llama.  When they campaigned, trailing for miles behind  their armies would be these endless baggage   trains of pack animals, llamas. The Aztecs had no equivalent.  Their only domestic animals were  the turkey and the Chihuahua.  Speaking of dogs, the conquistadors also brought  these big war mastiffs, these fighting dogs which   wore armor and were trained to take down men. Again, imagine the terrifying impact that   would have for the indigenous people. But the horse was the critical asset.  On attack, you could blast through any native  formation which didn’t have not just the weapons,   but the training or discipline to be  able to stand up to massed shock cavalry.  If things were going bad for the conquistadors,  they could retreat much faster than,   of course, the enemies could chase them. The Tlaxcalans appreciate all these assets coming   together, and they see this as their opportunity. They were the holdouts, the last remaining major   entity in Mesoamerica which was still  able to go toe-to-toe with the Aztecs.  They’d been completely surrounded. The Aztecs  were upping the ante every year with these   ceremonial flower wars, which were becoming  more and more obviously wars of conquest.  The Tlaxcalans had been cut off from  the coast and from sources of salt.  So they were being pushed to the brink. This is a Hail Mary for them. "If we ally   with these outsiders, these strangers, who  are just few in number after all, we may   have some potential way to break out of this  strategic trap that has been imposed upon us."  They lean over to the side of Cortés, and they  travel with him to Tenochtitlan, the capital,   the glittering jewel in the midst of Lake  Texcoco, the capital of the Aztec Empire.  Again, this is a dramatic moment when  Cortés passes through the causeways   out into the city and encounters Moctezuma  II, the huey tlatoani as he was called, the   Great Speaker, the emperor of the Aztec Empire. These two worlds come together at that moment.  The interface between them was Cortés’s  interpreter/mistress, Doña Marina,   Malinche as she became known, who is  translating from one side to the other.  The dialogue that occurs then is one of  those great tipping points in history.  What was the perspective of Moctezuma II? He was aware Cortés was coming.  This is his empire. He has envoys and  emissaries and scouts and spies everywhere.  They’re reporting back to him, "Something  has washed up on the shores of our empire,   and it is determined to meet with us." He initially bargains with Cortés,   urging him to leave. He provides him with precious gifts,   which of course just inflames Cortés even more. Once he’s got hold of Aztec gold, he’s just   determined to go all the way to the center. Moctezuma continues playing this double game.  His advisors, his council, urge him not  to allow Cortés to proceed to the capital.  His own brother, Cuitláhuac, tells him,  "If you allow this man inside your house,   he will take your house away from you." But Moctezuma proceeds, and for that he’s   been condemned by generations of historians. This was a mistake to bring the conquistadors   into the heart of the empire itself. I actually think that was his best option,   whether he was aware of it or not, because it  was better for him to have Cortés as his guest   within Tenochtitlan than it was to have Cortés,  this random element, at loose within his empire,   talking to the subject peoples, inflaming  them possibly against central authority.  He felt perhaps Cortés was what he said  he was, an envoy from a great emperor   on the far side of the vast ocean. Cortés, again with the mind games,   had no warrant to say he was a  diplomat or ambassador for anybody.  He kept telling anyone who’d listen, "I speak for  the mighty Charles V, the Holy Roman Emperor."  Of course, Charles V had no  idea who Hernán Cortés was.  Cortés, again, is just winging it,  just incredible improvisation here.  And for a moment… stasis. The great turning point comes   when word arrives from the coast that one  of the Aztec regional military officers,   on his own initiative, has taken action against  the conquistadors left behind on the coast,   the ones with the Totonacs, and  some of them have been killed.  Cortés seizes this as his pretext. He marches into the palace of Moctezuma II,   the Aztec huey tlatoani, and tells him that for  his own safety, he is now being taken under the   protective custody of the Spanish, and he should  come with him, or else there will be violence.  This is the moment when Moctezuma’s  entire worldview just collapses.  Nobody had spoken to him like this before. His psychology just disintegrates at that point,   and he meekly allows himself to be led away. He tells his people, "Don’t resist.  I don’t want bloodshed. I will  pass with these strangers."  Then once Cortés has rounded up the officers  from the coast responsible for turning on his men   there, he has them, in front of the emperor and  the entire court, burned alive, which is a form   of punishment totally unknown to the Aztecs. They watch this in grim silence.  Once Cortés has seized the emperor himself, once  he has Moctezuma, he already has the empire.  He governs through what is  increasingly becoming his puppet.  Moctezuma seems to have fallen almost under the  spell of Cortés, the classic Stockholm syndrome.  He gives him a grand tour of the city. Cortés, in again a subtle flex of his power,   has brigantines, small sailing boats, built. He takes Moctezuma with him on a sailing   cruise on Lake Texcoco, and the emperor’s  astonished at this new technology of using   the wind to sail on the water. Having the emperor was the key.  The emperor’s mistake wasn’t  inviting Cortés into the city.  It was making himself vulnerable by  staying there also in an adjacent palace.  If he had gone to some further location,  made some excuse, a pilgrimage or an   expedition of some kind, and had ruled through  subordinates, Cortés would’ve been baffled.  He couldn’t go chasing after the emperor. That would be obviously too provocative.  But without the emperor there, Cortés would  have had his options extremely limited.  I don’t know what he would’ve  done in that circumstance.  But because Moctezuma stayed in his  capital, he made himself the target.  Once he was taken, this was the key to  controlling the entire empire at that point.  Obviously the story continues  from there, with La Noche Triste.  What people might not appreciate about what  happened here, in both the Pizarro story of   the Inca Empire which we’ll talk about  later, and in the Aztec story, is that   in both cases the Spanish were themselves  divided and in fact fighting each other.  So maybe you should tell the story of  how Velázquez sends another expedition   to capture and arrest Cortés for going  beyond the prerogative of his mission.  We left the governor on Cuba, of course, fuming. He rallies another expeditionary force because   Cortés is stealing his thunder. He sends this under Pánfilo   de Narváez, a larger force than the  one Cortés brought with him originally.  This lands on the coast. Cortés appreciates he has to move, so   he leaves one of his subordinates, the hot-blooded  Alvarado, behind in charge in Tenochtitlan, takes   as many men as he can to the coast, confronts  de Narváez, and defeats him in a minor battle.  Again, diplomacy wins over  the entire expeditionary   force that the governor had dispatched. He tells them, "My friends, why are we fighting?  We have the empire at my disposal. Join with me and we can share in the riches."  So he wins over the vast  majority of this new force.  It effectively becomes reinforcements,  and he marches back to the capital.  He finds the mood has turned against him. The problem with being in charge is you   can’t be everywhere. His subordinate,   assuming that the Aztecs were mobilizing  against him, decided on a preemptive strike.  There was a festival. The aristocracy,  particularly the warrior caste,   were celebrating, and Alvarado just  descended on them and massacred everybody.  The survivors rally the population. When Cortés returns, he finds   himself effectively under siege. The people are so appalled now with   the failure of their huey tlatoani that when he  tries to pacify them, they throw stones at him.  Mortally wounded, he either dies  or the Spanish finish him off,   because he’s no longer of any use to them. Now Cortés is trapped in Tenochtitlan.  He determines to break out, and that is, as  you say, La Noche Triste, the Tragic Night,   because so many of his men are left behind. They’re either killed as they try to escape   the city across the causeways or forced to  retreat back to the palaces, where they’re   taken alive and sacrificed subsequently. Cortés gets away with a minority of   the troops still at his disposal and  makes it back to Tlaxcalan territory.  That was the critical aspect, the  two features of the entire campaign.  One, he has enough strike power with enough horses  to defeat the Aztecs when they try to finish him   off, at the Battle of Otumba. They feel he’s on the run.  They have the numbers. The  conquistadors are dragging   their tails between their legs as they flee. Cortés himself is grievously wounded. "We   can finish them off." They had the numbers.   They were winning. But again, Cortés  identifies where the Aztec general is.  He rallies enough horsemen to blast  through the Aztec ranks and take   out their command and control. The Aztec army disintegrates,   and the Spanish are able to flee. The battlefield advantages,   their horses, their steel, were critical,  but just as critical was the diplomacy.  If the Tlaxcalans had turned on Cortés  at that point, he would’ve been finished.  Not one Spaniard would’ve survived. None of them would’ve made it back to the coast.  But the Tlaxcalans, for their own reasons, not  out of any generosity or humanitarian impulse to   welcome back the conquistadors, still see, "We are  committed to these people and to our alliance."  So they give Cortés shelter. He recovers physically, begins to   rebuild his strength, and is determined to go back  to Tenochtitlan for round two: "This time we’re   not going to be indulging diplomatic niceties." The Tlaxcalans have their own perspective on this.  If you go to Tlaxcala, the territory today,  the governor’s mansion there has murals   on the wall, and these depict Cortés and the  conquistadors from the Tlaxcalan point of view.  It’s fascinating to look at how the relationship  is not between a superior and an inferior.  It’s between equals. You see them depicted in the  same scale, engaged in diplomacy between partners,   not between subordinates and dominant figures. The Tlaxcalans drove a hard bargain. "We want   territory carved out of the Aztecs. We want our own fortress in   Tenochtitlan after this is over." They saw this as them using the   conquistadors, not the other way around,  which is very important to bear in mind.  The Aztec Empire from a distance, if  you look at a map, seemed impressive.  But this was an imperial construct, and not  just the remaining independent entities like   the Tlaxcalans, like the Tarascans, who we  can discuss later, were hostile to the Aztecs.  So were so many of their subordinated peoples. The Totonacs on the coast, the Chalco states on   the shores of Lake Texcoco, they chafed  under Aztec hegemony and authority.  They too saw the conquistadors as an opportunity  to finally shrug off the authority and the demands   of the Aztecs, and get revenge in a lot of ways. Cortés builds up for the final campaign against   Tenochtitlan, against the new huey tlatoani,  Cuitláhuac, and then, after he died, his brother,   the last of the huey tlatoanis, Cuauhtémoc. He has indigenous people flocking to   his banner from all over Mesoamerica. He emphasizes that he’s still in the fight.  He still has those advantages. More reinforcements are arriving   at the coast, and they’re being  integrated into the conquistador army.  But of the force that marches on Tenochtitlan,  the conquistadors were maybe 0.5% in raw numbers.  The overwhelming majority were other  Mesoamerican peoples who see this as   their final reckoning with the Aztecs. This is the integration again of   the technology with the diplomacy. Cortés knows that to take the city,   he has to control the lake. Again, the innovations…   They need sulfur for their gunpowder. Their guns are useless without gunpowder.  So an expedition goes into the mountains  to the volcano, Popocatépetl, and they   dangle with ropes inside the caldera of the  volcano, scooping out the sulfur they need as   the critical ingredient for their gunpowder. Another one builds prefabricated brigantines,   boats, in their different sections, and then has  untold numbers of porters, human load-bearers,   bring these prefabricated pieces  over the mountains to the lake.  They’re assembled and let loose in the lake,  and now they have control over the lake.  Bringing together the technology and  the innovations with the local manpower,   this is the force directed against  Tenochtitlan in the final battle.  I actually didn’t know those stories. That’s crazy. One of the ways in which,   to the extent people are even aware of the story,  they might not understand what actually happened,   is that they have this model of the Aztecs  or the Incas as this cohesive single nation.  A better model might be something like,  imagine Russia and Ukraine have been   doing trench warfare for 100 years. Imagine the animosity, and then also   the Russians are taking tens of thousands of  Ukrainians and doing human sacrifices with them.  Then some foreign force comes in and says to the  Ukrainians, "We can help you march into Moscow."  I think they’d have pretty decent  odds of getting some agreement there.  The old phrase is, "The enemy  of my enemy is my friend,"   and in diplomacy and war, that’s always very true. I don't think I actually appreciated the ambition   of Jane Street's intern projects until last  week, when I got to see some of them for myself.  For example, one intern spent part of  his summer researching LLM memorization,   figuring out how to quantify and reduce it  without hurting out-of-sample performance.  This matters because whenever Jane Street  evaluates a new model on historical data,   they need to know that its performance  reflects predictive power, not just   memorization of past outcomes. Another intern built a custom   activation checkpointing scheme. Activation checkpointing lets you   trade compute for memory: you recalculate  some activations during backprop instead of   storing them all after the forward pass. This intern found a way to identify the   activations that are cheapest to recompute,  but that still free up a lot of memory.  And this allowed his version to  outperform PyTorch's native one.  These are just two examples, but Jane  Street has written about a bunch more.  These write-ups are coming out in batches. The first few are live now, including   these two, and the rest will be  published in the coming weeks.  If you want to read them, or if you want  to apply for Jane Street's 2027 summer   internships, go to janestreet.com/dwarkesh. There are so many interesting questions to ask,   everything from technology to  diplomacy to disease to tactics.  Before we get to that, just to round out the  story, in many ways what’s striking about the   conquest of the Incas in Peru under Pizarro 10  years later is how similar it was to Cortés’s   story, how much he just followed the playbook. I want people to have a sense of roughly what   happened here, starting with the Battle  of Cajamarca, which might be the most   astonishingly lopsided military encounter  that has maybe ever happened in human history.  If you can recapitulate at least that  battle a bit, and then the overall story,   then we can do some analysis from there. Absolutely. When Cortés consummates his   conquest of Tenochtitlan in 1521, the last  of the huey tlatoanis surrenders to him,   and he occupies the territory and, most  importantly, the top of the social hierarchy.  The existing structure, as much as  possible, is allowed to persist.  The conquistadors just decapitate the local  nobility and insert themselves at the top.  Now, this is the playbook that will continue  to be applied, less successfully, throughout   the rest of Mesoamerica because the existing  political entities there aren’t so sophisticated.  Nonetheless, there are rumors — there are  always rumors — of lost cities of gold.  More conquistadors are now flooding into  the New World to seek advantage of this.  One of these is a distant cousin  of Cortés named Francisco Pizarro.  He met with Cortés and got the playbook,  as you say, about how this is to be done.  Then, in one of these conquistador business  ventures, he finds the funding for men and   ships and begins pushing south down the west coast  of South America, crossing the equator and finally   arriving in what is now modern-day Peru. He encounters what he’s looking for:   a sophisticated culture on the scale… in fact, in  terms of territory, on a much broader scale than   Cortés had encountered in Mesoamerica. This is the land of the Inca.  When he arrived, there was civil war. The previous Sapa Inca, Huayna Capac,   had died in 1525, and his two sons,  Atahualpa and Huáscar, turned on each other.  Atahualpa had just won the civil war, and he  was proceeding to Cuzco, the Inca capital,   to be formally enthroned as the new Sapa Inca. That’s when word arrives to him that strangers   have entered his realm. Again, we’re talking 168 men   who have pushed into the Andes Mountains  and are seeking him out for reasons unknown.  He encounters them outside a place  called, as you say, Cajamarca in 1532.  He sees not threat, but opportunity. Just like Moctezuma II had been advised   not to treat with these people, so does  Atahualpa’s envoy, who reports to him,   "These are not men of good faith. We can take them out.  They tend to sleep together. At night, we can set fire to   wherever they’re staying and just  take them all out in one fell swoop."  But Atahualpa is interested in  what they have to offer him.  He’s seen the horses. In fact,  Pizarro made a specific case of   impressing the Sapa Inca with his horses. He sends one of his key lieutenants to put   on a display of horsemanship. Famously, he charges right at   the Sapa Inca and all his court. The horse stops just inches from   Atahualpa’s face, snorting and breathing. Atahualpa is absolutely stony-faced and   professes to be unimpressed and says, "I will  meet with your master at a time of my choosing."  After the Spaniards leave, he has all of his  court, including his generals who flinched or   showed fear, executed just to make the point,  "We’re not to be intimidated by these people."  He sends a blocking force, tens of  thousands of men, to cut off any retreat,   and then he proceeds to meet with Pizarro at  Cajamarca with the vast expanse of his army.  There’s a saying in Peru that Atahualpa  was planning to have Pizarro for lunch,   but Pizarro ended up having him for breakfast. Once he enters into the confines of a narrow,   constricted courtyard space, that’s  when Pizarro lets off the ambush.  He lets fly with all his artillery  and all his musketry for the shock   value, and unleashes his horses. Atahualpa himself is overwhelmed   and taken prisoner at that point. This again is the playbook,   the copybook, as you say. Go to the top. Seize whoever is at   the very pinnacle of the social hierarchy. You control the entire structure.  Just so people know the numbers here, the Incan  Empire overall has some 10 million inhabitants.  During this first battle where Pizarro encounters  the emperor, he has some 160-190 conquistadors.  I don’t think the numbers are known  for exactly how many Atahualpa had,   but he’s facing off against the  army that has just clinched the   civil war in the Inca Empire,  and it’s tens of thousands big.  I’ve seen some numbers that  are like 100,000 or 200,000,   but certainly in the high tens of thousands. So 100-something against almost 100,000.  That’s the first battle. What is astonishing  is that these 100 conquistadors kill… I saw   some numbers that are like 10,000 of the enemy,  or at least thousands of Atahualpa’s troops.  They suffer zero casualties. So they kill close  to 10,000 of the enemy and suffer zero casualties.  This is the first encounter that the Inca  Empire has ever had with the conquistadors.  That must have been shocking  from both sides’ perspective.  If you can do some analysis  here, how is it possible?  How can you have a military outcome where you have  literally a KD ratio of infinity: 10,000 to zero?  The conquistadors themselves admitted that  the night before that encounter, there were   so many campfires from the Inca army scattered  across the hills surrounding Cajamarca that it   looked like the twinkling of stars at night. The conquistadors themselves admitted that when   they saw the number of Inca troops filing  into this courtyard, they were losing control   of their own bladders out of fear. They knew what the risks were here.  But the shock value of that initial  impetus was enough to carry them through.  The Inca had never heard gunpowder  weapons fired in any format before.  The ancestral founder of their empire was  Pachacuti, which means the thunder bearer.  But to see a real-world exemplar of  that must have been beyond shocking.  The actual physical damage that the cannons and  arquebuses inflicted was relatively minor, but   the explosion and the fact that these strangers  seemed able to control the thunder must have been   psychologically devastating. Then it came down again to   that steel and those horses. When Pizarro unleashed the horses,   this is something that the Inca… As you say, these  are veteran warriors, the winners of a civil war,   strategists at a tactical level within the  framework of pre-Columbian Andean warfare.  They were the top dogs, but  this is something outside   of their entire understanding of the universe. They’d never seen a horse before or knew what it   could do if you integrate a rider into the saddle  with stirrups and the shock value of that charge.  They had no doctrine to push back against that. The psychological impact was   that they tried to flee. They were piling up against   the walls in their desperation to scramble over  them, to the point where the walls finally gave   way under the press of all those bodies. Some of them escaped into the countryside,   and the Spaniards rode after them,  just running them down as they fled.  The only thing that stopped the massacre  at the end was that night was falling,   and the Spaniards in the darkness  couldn’t continue the pursuit any longer.  It’s what happens when something totally  outside the universe of even veteran warriors   plays out in a way that they have no mental  appreciation of, or are unable to draw on any kind   of library of how to respond to the situation. They   would almost keep the helmets to protect the  head, but many of them were ditching the metal   armor in favor of the local stuff because that was  good enough as protection against local weapons.  They would not have done that  and carried it back to Europe.  That would have made them too vulnerable. But here you adapt to the circumstances.  You have more freedom of mobility. It’s less exhausting wearing   cotton than it is to wear metal. They would make that adaptation.  They would even sometimes, for very prized  allies, again as a way of integrating them   into the Spanish coalition, provide local  chiefs and warlords with Spanish weapons,   just to emphasize, "You’re so special to me." This was effective in binding them together.  They were very, very clever in identifying  the local sub-chiefs beneath the Aztec layer   of authority who would be receptive to  the idea of, "Why are you taking orders   from them when you get a better deal from us?" There was that seductive   quality at the elite level. Now, what they didn’t understand — so   many of them thinking they were using  the Spanish to their advantage — they   didn’t appreciate the numbers in which the  Spanish and later Europeans would arrive.  Their closed worlds didn’t allow them  to think that people from such vast   distances could come in such huge numbers. This is such a bizarre and shocking and   interesting part of human  history, and I appreciate you   coming on and telling us all about it. Real pleasure. Thank you for having me.

I want to talk to you about the  conquest of the Aztec and the Inca
Empires because these are some of the  most shocking events in human history,
unparalleled among all the military  and diplomatic achievements ever made.
A few hundred conquistadors show up to  a new continent they know nothing about.
Within a matter of years, they subjugate empires  which have millions of inhabitants in them.
In the process of doing so, they are often winning  battles where they are outnumbered 100 to 1,
1,000 to 1, and in many cases not  even taking a single casualty.
They’re doing this while upwards of 99% of their  fighting forces are made up of the very natives
that they’re going to subjugate. I wanted to have you on to talk
about something this episode. We’re not going to focus on it,
we’re mostly talking about history here,  but people think of AI takeover as this
crazy sci-fi scenario but this would not be the  first time in history that an alien force, with
motivations that the natives don’t understand, is  able to use diplomatic cunning and technological
advantages to outmaneuver and then take over  a much larger and well-established order.
I wanted to have you on to  understand what happened here.
First, I would love to hear the stories. What did Cortés do? What did Pizarro do?
How did these conquests actually go down? Thank you. It’s a great pleasure to be here.
Yes, we’re talking about the birth of our modern  world, which played out between 600 to 500
years ago and created the modern globalized  community that we all participate in today.
It began in the 15th century when Europe,  backed up against the wall of the Atlantic,
under immense pressure from external forces and  cut off from the core economic power bases of the
East — the sources of the spice and silk that had  driven the global economy historically throughout
Eurasia — was finally forced to innovate. Key names like Prince Henry the Navigator
of Portugal work on turning the Atlantic  Ocean from a barrier into a superhighway.
Generational knowledge accrued from captains  reporting on tides and wind currents and whatever
land they’ve managed to reconnoiter, building out  the map as they go along, enables them to find a
way around the southern tip of Africa directly  to India and therefore cut out the middleman.
The Spanish, meanwhile, are heading west. We all know the story of Christopher Columbus:
"In 1492, he sailed the ocean blue." That was entrepreneurship. This
was an expedition to arrive at the  Oriental markets by traveling west.
Of course, his figures were completely wrong. He was saved by the fact that, unknown to him,
there was an entire continent in the  place where he thought Japan, China,
and the Spice Islands would be. Initially, that was perceived,
ironically, as a disappointment. But over time, it became increasingly
apparent this was a source of potential in land,  in wealth, and in people that could be exploited.
A key turning point happened in 1511 when  an ambitious Spanish nobleman, de Velázquez,
seizes control of Cuba. He sends out from this power
base expeditions exploring the coast of what  we would call Mesoamerica, Central America.
Later in 1518, he assigns that task to a man  with whom he’s had a somewhat tempestuous
relationship, a man named Hernán Cortés. He’d arrived in the New World in Cuba in 1511.
He had some legal training, so he served as a  notary and worked his way up to being alcalde,
which is chief magistrate, on Cuba. But he had much greater ambition.
He takes this warrant from  the governor and runs with it.
He begins recruiting men to a much wider and  much more ambitious goal: not just to explore
the coast, but to penetrate into the interior, to  find out what’s there, and to seize control of it.
When the governor realizes what  Cortés is up to, he tries to stop him.
There’s this great moment on 18th November 1518. He arrives at the waterfront just as Cortés gets
into a boat to go out to his ships offshore. The governor calls out to him,
"What are you up to?" Cortés assures him, "Don’t worry.
I have this all under control." But of course, the governor
had lost control at that point. Now it was Cortés’s expedition.
This is the background. Again, as you say, he  is literally going off the side of the map.
He’s entering terra incognita,  unknown to Europeans previously.
His political antenna, honed by years in the  islands, enables him to appreciate at a very early
stage that there is a significant imperial power  which has hegemony here in the mainland, and that
its subject peoples chafe under the authority  of whoever this lord or imperial power is.
He arrives in the lands of the Totonacs, who had  recently been incorporated into the imperial orbit
of a people who call themselves the Mexica  — hence Mexico as we know it — but who have
come down to history based on their mythical  origins in a land called Aztlán as the Aztecs.
For simplicity’s sake, that’s  what we’ll refer to them as.
The Totonacs resented this authority, as  all subjugated and subordinated peoples do,
and they saw the arrival of these outsiders  as a potential opportunity to throw off the
authority that had been imposed on them. Having established this relationship with
the Totonacs, Cortés begins to march inland, and  he enters the territory of the Tlaxcalans, who,
like an autoimmune system, immediately rallied  to defeat him, to expel him from their territory.
But he fights them to a standstill for such  a period of time that the Tlaxcalans and he
arrive at a new kind of arrangement. The Tlaxcalans again appreciate his
strength, his power, his potential. They swing over to his side and will
henceforward serve as guides and reinforcements  for his expedition deeper into the interior.
Can we pause here and talk about the numbers? How many men had Cortés brought with him?
Even the Tlaxcalans had much  larger numbers than Cortés did.
So even the standstill is an impressive  military achievement, especially because
he’s fighting without native support. What are the numbers even at this point?
A few hundred on Cortés’ side and multiple  thousands on the Tlaxcalans’ side.
It’s at this point that the critical  technological differentials from the Old
and New World really begin to come into effect. The classic text which got me invested in this
whole scenario in the first place is Jared  Diamond’s book, Guns, Germs, and Steel.
He enumerates in the title those critical  advantages that the Spaniards had.
Guns in reality weren’t so significant. Once the Native peoples got over the shock value,
they appreciated, given the very slow reloading  times involved in firearms at that time,
that they weren’t so significant  as assets on the battlefield.
But steel was critical. Local weapons were carved  from wood and from stone and from obsidian, that
volcanic glass which is razor sharp when honed to  a point and quite dangerous as a slashing weapon.
But against the steel armor, and especially the  steel helmets that the conquistadors were wearing,
it was much less effective. The conquistadors were drawing
on military traditions of the Old World  that went back generations, incorporating
long Toledo steel sword blades. They used those as thrusting weapons to take
out indigenous warriors who were coming in with  cut-and-slash weapons, which of course open up
the side of the body to be taken out very early. The combination of the technology with generations
of inherited military training and  skill meant that the conquistadors
had that critical edge on the battlefield. Now, they weren’t invincible. Cortés was again
playing those mind games. He was taking casualties,
and he was careful to bury his dead underneath  the houses that they were sheltering in so the
Tlaxcalans wouldn’t be aware that they were even  having some successes in hand-to-hand combat.
It was as much a mind game  as it was a physical game.
The ultimate weapon, of course, that the  conquistadors brought with them was their horses.
I cannot overemphasize how vital the horse was  to the conquistadors once they entered into the
interior of the American continents. They had the external asset.
They had sail power, which enabled them  to land anywhere they wanted on the coast.
But in the interior, the horse was decisive. There were no native equivalents.
The horse originated in North America,  but it had subsequently died out.
The local peoples had not just no  horses, but no beast of burden generally.
That was not integrated into their economies,  into their ways of life, or into their military.
The Inca, whom we’ll discuss in a moment,  did have one, which was the llama.
When they campaigned, trailing for miles behind  their armies would be these endless baggage
trains of pack animals, llamas. The Aztecs had no equivalent.
Their only domestic animals were  the turkey and the Chihuahua.
Speaking of dogs, the conquistadors also brought  these big war mastiffs, these fighting dogs which
wore armor and were trained to take down men. Again, imagine the terrifying impact that
would have for the indigenous people. But the horse was the critical asset.
On attack, you could blast through any native  formation which didn’t have not just the weapons,
but the training or discipline to be  able to stand up to massed shock cavalry.
If things were going bad for the conquistadors,  they could retreat much faster than,
of course, the enemies could chase them. The Tlaxcalans appreciate all these assets coming
together, and they see this as their opportunity. They were the holdouts, the last remaining major
entity in Mesoamerica which was still  able to go toe-to-toe with the Aztecs.
They’d been completely surrounded. The Aztecs  were upping the ante every year with these
ceremonial flower wars, which were becoming  more and more obviously wars of conquest.
The Tlaxcalans had been cut off from  the coast and from sources of salt.
So they were being pushed to the brink. This is a Hail Mary for them. "If we ally
with these outsiders, these strangers, who  are just few in number after all, we may
have some potential way to break out of this  strategic trap that has been imposed upon us."
They lean over to the side of Cortés, and they  travel with him to Tenochtitlan, the capital,
the glittering jewel in the midst of Lake  Texcoco, the capital of the Aztec Empire.
Again, this is a dramatic moment when  Cortés passes through the causeways
out into the city and encounters Moctezuma  II, the huey tlatoani as he was called, the
Great Speaker, the emperor of the Aztec Empire. These two worlds come together at that moment.
The interface between them was Cortés’s  interpreter/mistress, Doña Marina,
Malinche as she became known, who is  translating from one side to the other.
The dialogue that occurs then is one of  those great tipping points in history.
What was the perspective of Moctezuma II? He was aware Cortés was coming.
This is his empire. He has envoys and  emissaries and scouts and spies everywhere.
They’re reporting back to him, "Something  has washed up on the shores of our empire,
and it is determined to meet with us." He initially bargains with Cortés,
urging him to leave. He provides him with precious gifts,
which of course just inflames Cortés even more. Once he’s got hold of Aztec gold, he’s just
determined to go all the way to the center. Moctezuma continues playing this double game.
His advisors, his council, urge him not  to allow Cortés to proceed to the capital.
His own brother, Cuitláhuac, tells him,  "If you allow this man inside your house,
he will take your house away from you." But Moctezuma proceeds, and for that he’s
been condemned by generations of historians. This was a mistake to bring the conquistadors

whether he was aware of it or not, because it  was better for him to have Cortés as his guest
within Tenochtitlan than it was to have Cortés,  this random element, at loose within his empire,
talking to the subject peoples, inflaming  them possibly against central authority.
He felt perhaps Cortés was what he said  he was, an envoy from a great emperor
on the far side of the vast ocean. Cortés, again with the mind games,
had no warrant to say he was a  diplomat or ambassador for anybody.
He kept telling anyone who’d listen, "I speak for  the mighty Charles V, the Holy Roman Emperor."
Of course, Charles V had no  idea who Hernán Cortés was.
Cortés, again, is just winging it,  just incredible improvisation here.
And for a moment… stasis. The great turning point comes
when word arrives from the coast that one  of the Aztec regional military officers,
on his own initiative, has taken action against  the conquistadors left behind on the coast,
the ones with the Totonacs, and  some of them have been killed.
Cortés seizes this as his pretext. He marches into the palace of Moctezuma II,
the Aztec huey tlatoani, and tells him that for  his own safety, he is now being taken under the
protective custody of the Spanish, and he should  come with him, or else there will be violence.
This is the moment when Moctezuma’s  entire worldview just collapses.
Nobody had spoken to him like this before. His psychology just disintegrates at that point,
and he meekly allows himself to be led away. He tells his people, "Don’t resist.
I don’t want bloodshed. I will  pass with these strangers."
Then once Cortés has rounded up the officers  from the coast responsible for turning on his men
there, he has them, in front of the emperor and  the entire court, burned alive, which is a form
of punishment totally unknown to the Aztecs. They watch this in grim silence.
Once Cortés has seized the emperor himself, once  he has Moctezuma, he already has the empire.
He governs through what is  increasingly becoming his puppet.
Moctezuma seems to have fallen almost under the  spell of Cortés, the classic Stockholm syndrome.
He gives him a grand tour of the city. Cortés, in again a subtle flex of his power,
has brigantines, small sailing boats, built. He takes Moctezuma with him on a sailing
cruise on Lake Texcoco, and the emperor’s  astonished at this new technology of using
the wind to sail on the water. Having the emperor was the key.
The emperor’s mistake wasn’t  inviting Cortés into the city.
It was making himself vulnerable by  staying there also in an adjacent palace.
If he had gone to some further location,  made some excuse, a pilgrimage or an
expedition of some kind, and had ruled through  subordinates, Cortés would’ve been baffled.
He couldn’t go chasing after the emperor. That would be obviously too provocative.
But without the emperor there, Cortés would  have had his options extremely limited.
I don’t know what he would’ve  done in that circumstance.
But because Moctezuma stayed in his  capital, he made himself the target.
Once he was taken, this was the key to  controlling the entire empire at that point.
Obviously the story continues  from there, with La Noche Triste.
What people might not appreciate about what  happened here, in both the Pizarro story of
the Inca Empire which we’ll talk about  later, and in the Aztec story, is that
in both cases the Spanish were themselves  divided and in fact fighting each other.
So maybe you should tell the story of  how Velázquez sends another expedition
to capture and arrest Cortés for going  beyond the prerogative of his mission.
We left the governor on Cuba, of course, fuming. He rallies another expeditionary force because
Cortés is stealing his thunder. He sends this under Pánfilo
de Narváez, a larger force than the  one Cortés brought with him originally.
This lands on the coast. Cortés appreciates he has to move, so
he leaves one of his subordinates, the hot-blooded  Alvarado, behind in charge in Tenochtitlan, takes
as many men as he can to the coast, confronts  de Narváez, and defeats him in a minor battle.
Again, diplomacy wins over  the entire expeditionary
force that the governor had dispatched. He tells them, "My friends, why are we fighting?
We have the empire at my disposal. Join with me and we can share in the riches."
So he wins over the vast  majority of this new force.
It effectively becomes reinforcements,  and he marches back to the capital.
He finds the mood has turned against him. The problem with being in charge is you
can’t be everywhere. His subordinate,
assuming that the Aztecs were mobilizing  against him, decided on a preemptive strike.
There was a festival. The aristocracy,  particularly the warrior caste,
were celebrating, and Alvarado just  descended on them and massacred everybody.
The survivors rally the population. When Cortés returns, he finds
himself effectively under siege. The people are so appalled now with
the failure of their huey tlatoani that when he  tries to pacify them, they throw stones at him.
Mortally wounded, he either dies  or the Spanish finish him off,
because he’s no longer of any use to them. Now Cortés is trapped in Tenochtitlan.
He determines to break out, and that is, as  you say, La Noche Triste, the Tragic Night,
because so many of his men are left behind. They’re either killed as they try to escape
the city across the causeways or forced to  retreat back to the palaces, where they’re
taken alive and sacrificed subsequently. Cortés gets away with a minority of
the troops still at his disposal and  makes it back to Tlaxcalan territory.
That was the critical aspect, the  two features of the entire campaign.
One, he has enough strike power with enough horses  to defeat the Aztecs when they try to finish him
off, at the Battle of Otumba. They feel he’s on the run.
They have the numbers. The  conquistadors are dragging
their tails between their legs as they flee. Cortés himself is grievously wounded. "We
can finish them off." They had the numbers.
They were winning. But again, Cortés  identifies where the Aztec general is.
He rallies enough horsemen to blast  through the Aztec ranks and take
out their command and control. The Aztec army disintegrates,
and the Spanish are able to flee. The battlefield advantages,
their horses, their steel, were critical,  but just as critical was the diplomacy.
If the Tlaxcalans had turned on Cortés  at that point, he would’ve been finished.
Not one Spaniard would’ve survived. None of them would’ve made it back to the coast.
But the Tlaxcalans, for their own reasons, not  out of any generosity or humanitarian impulse to
welcome back the conquistadors, still see, "We are  committed to these people and to our alliance."
So they give Cortés shelter. He recovers physically, begins to
rebuild his strength, and is determined to go back  to Tenochtitlan for round two: "This time we’re
not going to be indulging diplomatic niceties." The Tlaxcalans have their own perspective on this.
If you go to Tlaxcala, the territory today,  the governor’s mansion there has murals
on the wall, and these depict Cortés and the  conquistadors from the Tlaxcalan point of view.
It’s fascinating to look at how the relationship  is not between a superior and an inferior.
It’s between equals. You see them depicted in the  same scale, engaged in diplomacy between partners,
not between subordinates and dominant figures. The Tlaxcalans drove a hard bargain. "We want
territory carved out of the Aztecs. We want our own fortress in
Tenochtitlan after this is over." They saw this as them using the
conquistadors, not the other way around,  which is very important to bear in mind.
The Aztec Empire from a distance, if  you look at a map, seemed impressive.
But this was an imperial construct, and not  just the remaining independent entities like
the Tlaxcalans, like the Tarascans, who we  can discuss later, were hostile to the Aztecs.
So were so many of their subordinated peoples. The Totonacs on the coast, the Chalco states on
the shores of Lake Texcoco, they chafed  under Aztec hegemony and authority.
They too saw the conquistadors as an opportunity  to finally shrug off the authority and the demands
of the Aztecs, and get revenge in a lot of ways. Cortés builds up for the final campaign against
Tenochtitlan, against the new huey tlatoani,  Cuitláhuac, and then, after he died, his brother,
the last of the huey tlatoanis, Cuauhtémoc. He has indigenous people flocking to
his banner from all over Mesoamerica. He emphasizes that he’s still in the fight.
He still has those advantages. More reinforcements are arriving
at the coast, and they’re being  integrated into the conquistador army.
But of the force that marches on Tenochtitlan,  the conquistadors were maybe 0.5% in raw numbers.
The overwhelming majority were other  Mesoamerican peoples who see this as
their final reckoning with the Aztecs. This is the integration again of
the technology with the diplomacy. Cortés knows that to take the city,
he has to control the lake. Again, the innovations…
They need sulfur for their gunpowder. Their guns are useless without gunpowder.
So an expedition goes into the mountains  to the volcano, Popocatépetl, and they
dangle with ropes inside the caldera of the  volcano, scooping out the sulfur they need as
the critical ingredient for their gunpowder. Another one builds prefabricated brigantines,
boats, in their different sections, and then has  untold numbers of porters, human load-bearers,
bring these prefabricated pieces  over the mountains to the lake.
They’re assembled and let loose in the lake,  and now they have control over the lake.
Bringing together the technology and  the innovations with the local manpower,
this is the force directed against  Tenochtitlan in the final battle.
I actually didn’t know those stories. That’s crazy. One of the ways in which,

story, how much he just followed the playbook. I want people to have a sense of roughly what
happened here, starting with the Battle  of Cajamarca, which might be the most

If you can recapitulate at least that  battle a bit, and then the overall story,

and he occupies the territory and, most  importantly, the top of the social hierarchy.
The existing structure, as much as  possible, is allowed to persist.
The conquistadors just decapitate the local  nobility and insert themselves at the top.
Now, this is the playbook that will continue  to be applied, less successfully, throughout
the rest of Mesoamerica because the existing  political entities there aren’t so sophisticated.
Nonetheless, there are rumors — there are  always rumors — of lost cities of gold.
More conquistadors are now flooding into  the New World to seek advantage of this.
One of these is a distant cousin  of Cortés named Francisco Pizarro.
He met with Cortés and got the playbook,  as you say, about how this is to be done.
Then, in one of these conquistador business  ventures, he finds the funding for men and
ships and begins pushing south down the west coast  of South America, crossing the equator and finally
arriving in what is now modern-day Peru. He encounters what he’s looking for:
a sophisticated culture on the scale… in fact, in  terms of territory, on a much broader scale than
Cortés had encountered in Mesoamerica. This is the land of the Inca.
When he arrived, there was civil war. The previous Sapa Inca, Huayna Capac,
had died in 1525, and his two sons,  Atahualpa and Huáscar, turned on each other.
Atahualpa had just won the civil war, and he  was proceeding to Cuzco, the Inca capital,
to be formally enthroned as the new Sapa Inca. That’s when word arrives to him that strangers
have entered his realm. Again, we’re talking 168 men
who have pushed into the Andes Mountains  and are seeking him out for reasons unknown.
He encounters them outside a place  called, as you say, Cajamarca in 1532.
He sees not threat, but opportunity. Just like Moctezuma II had been advised
not to treat with these people, so does  Atahualpa’s envoy, who reports to him,
"These are not men of good faith. We can take them out.
They tend to sleep together. At night, we can set fire to
wherever they’re staying and just  take them all out in one fell swoop."
But Atahualpa is interested in  what they have to offer him.
He’s seen the horses. In fact,  Pizarro made a specific case of
impressing the Sapa Inca with his horses. He sends one of his key lieutenants to put
on a display of horsemanship. Famously, he charges right at
the Sapa Inca and all his court. The horse stops just inches from
Atahualpa’s face, snorting and breathing. Atahualpa is absolutely stony-faced and
professes to be unimpressed and says, "I will  meet with your master at a time of my choosing."
After the Spaniards leave, he has all of his  court, including his generals who flinched or
showed fear, executed just to make the point,  "We’re not to be intimidated by these people."
He sends a blocking force, tens of  thousands of men, to cut off any retreat,
and then he proceeds to meet with Pizarro at  Cajamarca with the vast expanse of his army.
There’s a saying in Peru that Atahualpa  was planning to have Pizarro for lunch,
but Pizarro ended up having him for breakfast. Once he enters into the confines of a narrow,
constricted courtyard space, that’s  when Pizarro lets off the ambush.
He lets fly with all his artillery  and all his musketry for the shock
value, and unleashes his horses. Atahualpa himself is overwhelmed
and taken prisoner at that point. This again is the playbook,
the copybook, as you say. Go to the top. Seize whoever is at
the very pinnacle of the social hierarchy. You control the entire structure.
Just so people know the numbers here, the Incan  Empire overall has some 10 million inhabitants.
During this first battle where Pizarro encounters  the emperor, he has some 160-190 conquistadors.
I don’t think the numbers are known  for exactly how many Atahualpa had,
but he’s facing off against the  army that has just clinched the
civil war in the Inca Empire,  and it’s tens of thousands big.
